Daily, weekly and monthly prices

PTF is the hourly price set in the day-ahead market (GÖP). AOF is the volume-weighted average price of trades in the intraday market (GİP), from July 2015. SMF is the price of the last balancing instruction the system operator used in each hour (DGP). All three are averages of hourly prices in Turkish lira. The dashed line is the price cap in force (the average cap in the period for weekly and monthly views); it starts on 1 April 2022, and the price limits section below explains it. Use the buttons to change the time step and the range; click a name in the legend to hide or show a line.

The long view in euros

The yearly average PTF in lira was about 18 times higher in 2025 than in 2012, mostly because of inflation and the weaker lira, so a long lira series hides real changes. EPİAŞ also publishes every hourly PTF in euros and US dollars, converted at that day’s exchange rate. The chart shows weekly averages in either currency. The dashed line is the price cap in that currency: the lira cap divided by the exchange rate implied by each day’s PTF, so it moves with the exchange rate even when the lira cap is unchanged. It starts on 1 April 2022, when the cap became a fixed amount; before that it followed a formula. Switch to Log to compare changes in percentage terms: on a log scale a doubling looks the same in 2013 and in 2022, so quieter years are no longer flattened by the 2022 gas crisis.

Yearly figures are simple averages of hourly prices: every hour counts the same. SMF starts in April 2014 on the transparency platform, AOF in July 2015 when the intraday market opened. “Hours system short” is the share of hours in which the system needed extra energy (Enerji Açığı), so balancing instructions were mostly to increase output.

Where electricity is traded

Electricity changes hands in three places: bilateral contracts (İA) agreed directly between companies, the day-ahead market (GÖP) run by EPİAŞ, and the intraday market (GİP), where positions are adjusted up to shortly before delivery. Bilateral volume counts every contract, including resales between traders, so traded volume is larger than consumption. Volumes are published from December 2017.

The day-ahead market is where the reference price is set, but most electricity is sold through bilateral contracts. The intraday market is small: a few percent of traded volume, used to correct positions as forecasts change.

Price limits: a cap and a floor

Offers and prices in the day-ahead market must stay between a minimum and a maximum set by the regulator, EPDK. The minimum has always been zero. The maximum has changed many times; the balancing market (SMF) works under the same limits. Both are published in the Official Gazette.

Why a cap? The decisions we read state the limit but not the reasoning, so this part is our reading of press reports and of the market’s structure. A cap limits what one hour can cost buyers when supply is tight, when a few large plants set the price, or when gas costs jump with the exchange rate. Until spring 2022 the cap followed a formula: three times the trailing twelve-month weighted average PTF, and at most 2,000 TL/MWh, so it rose as prices rose. Since 1 April 2022 it is a fixed amount in lira that the board changes by decision.

Why a floor at zero? Bids below zero are not accepted, so the price cannot go negative. Most European day-ahead markets allow negative prices, with a harmonised minimum of −500 EUR/MWh in the coupled EU market at the time of writing (a regulatory limit that can change). In Türkiye the decisions simply state a minimum of 0. When must-run and renewable output exceeds demand, the price sits at zero, so zero-price hours show that there is a surplus but not how large it is.

What the limits do to the data. At the cap or the floor the price stops carrying information about scarcity or surplus: it is cut off, not observed. Averages, spreads and volatility measures are therefore likely to be smaller than they would be without limits, and a cap that is hit often shapes the whole price distribution; the chart below shows how often.

In the last 12 months, PTF reached the cap in at least one hour on 45% of days (164 of 365). The cap in force on 13 November 2026 is 4,500 TL/MWh, about 81 EUR/MWh at the average exchange rate of the last 30 days. At its highest in euros (Sep 2022) it was about 272 EUR/MWh. Increases in the lira cap have not kept pace with the lira’s fall, so the cap is lower in euros than it was.

Before 1 April 2022 the cap was formula-based, so the fixed-cap table above does not reach back further. The monthly maximum prices of July 2021 to March 2022 rise in steps (617, 636, 674, 718 and then 1,078 to 1,745 TL/MWh) and equal the daily maximum on most days, which fits a cap that was rebuilt each month; we have not verified the formula’s start date, so hours at the cap are not counted for that period.
